{{Short description|Movement to end constitutional monarchy in Canada}}
{{Use Canadian English|date=July 2026}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2020}}
[[File:CCR ottawa chapter 2005.jpg|300px|thumb|right|A demonstration on [[Parliament Hill]] by members of [[Citizens for a Canadian Republic]] during the installation ceremony of [[Governor General of Canada|Governor General]] [[Michaëlle Jean]], 2005]]
{{Republicanism sidebar}}

'''Republicanism in Canada''' or '''Canadian Republicanism''' is a movement for the replacement of the [[monarchy of Canada]] and a monarch as [[head of state]] with a [[parliamentary republic]] and a democratically selected Canadian as head of state. Republicans are driven by various factors, such as a perception of inequality in the concept of excluding all but members of the [[Monarchy of Canada#Royal family and house|royal family]] from the position or the argument that [[Patriation|Canadian independence]] will not be achieved until Canadians can choose their own head of state independently and democratically.<ref name=CCRgoals>{{cite web| url=https://www.canadian-republic.ca/goals| title=Our Goals| publisher=Citizens for a Canadian Republic| access-date=22 May 2022}}</ref>

As with [[monarchism in Canada]], strong [[republicanism]] is not a prevalent element of contemporary Canadian society. The movement's roots precede [[Canadian Confederation]] and it has emerged from time to time in Canadian politics, but has not been an influential force since the [[Rebellions of 1837]],<ref>{{Cite book| last=Coates| first=Colin MacMillan| title=Majesty in Canada: essays on the role of royalty| publisher=Dundurn Press Ltd.| year=2006| location=Toronto| page=11| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FhFyvhpPx8MC| isbn=978-1-55002-586-6}}</ref> which some Canadian republicans consider their efforts to be a continuation of.<ref>{{Cite book| last=White| first=Randall| date=20 May 2002| contribution=Address by Randall White, PhD, Political Science author, policy analyst and observer to the Executive Committee of Citizens for a Canadian Republic| contribution-url=http://www.canadian-republic.ca/speech_rw_3_20_02.html| editor-last=Citizens for a Canadian Republic| editor-link=Citizens for a Canadian Republic| title=About CCR > Speeches and commentary| place=Toronto| publisher=Citizens for a Canadian Republic| access-date=3 September 2009| archive-date=14 June 2020| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200614060051/http://www.canadian-republic.ca/speech_rw_3_20_02.html| url-status=dead}}</ref>

==National identity==
{{rquote|right|Monarchy and inherited rights in government, symbolic or otherwise, is a concept incompatible with Canadian values of egalitarianism.|[[Citizens for a Canadian Republic]]}}

Republicans in Canada assert that because of its [[Heredity|hereditary]] aspects, the monarchy is inherently contrary to [[egalitarianism]] and [[multiculturalism in Canada|multiculturalism]].<ref name=OC>{{Cite news| title=The fight for the Republic of Canada| newspaper=Ottawa Citizen| date=19 November 2004| url=http://www.canada.com/national/features/democracy/story.html?id=%7B1F3EF50E-2A74-401B-883E-AD27A04B271A%7D| access-date=18 September 2009| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090808052403/http://www2.canada.com/national/features/democracy/story.html?id=%7B1f3ef50e-2a74-401b-883e-ad27a04b271a%7D| archive-date=8 August 2009}}</ref> Further, though it diverges from both the official position of the [[Government of Canada|Canadian government]] and the stated opinions of some judges, legal scholars,<ref name=MacLeod17>{{Cite book| last=MacLeod| first=Kevin S.| author-link=Kevin S. This questioning of the monarchy's role in [[Canadian identity]] arose as a part of wider cultural changes that followed the evolution of the British Empire into the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], the rise of [[anti-establishment]]ism, the creation of [[multiculturalism]] as an [[Official Policy|official policy]] in Canada, and the blossoming of [[Quebec sovereignty movement|Quebec separatism]]; the latter becoming the major impetus of political controversy around the Crown.<ref name=Phillips19>{{cite journal|last=Phillips |first=Stephen |title=Republicanism in Canada in the Reign of Elizabeth II: the Dog that Didn't Bark |journal=Canadian Monarchist News |volume=Summer 2004 |issue=22 |page=19 |publisher=Monarchist League of Canada |location=Toronto |year=2004 |url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2004/Sum04PDFRepublicanism.pdf |access-date=13 September 2009 |ref=CITEREF_Phillips_2004 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708032249/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2004/Sum04PDFRepublicanism.pdf |archive-date=8 July 2009 }}</ref> Quebec nationalists agitated for an independent Quebec republic and the monarchy was targeted as a symbol of anti-[[English-speaking Quebecker|Anglophone]] demonstration,<ref>{{cite book| last=Speaight| first=Robert| title=Vanier, Soldier, Diplomat, Governor General: A Biography| publisher=Collins| year=1970| location=London| isbn=978-0-00-262252-3| url=https://archive.org/details/vaniersoldierdip00spea}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://archive.org/details/ecritspolemiques0000bour| isbn=978-2-89005-158-4}}</ref> notably Quebecers turned their backs on her procession when she toured [[Quebec City]] that year.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.cbc.ca/archives/categories/society/the-monarchy/canadas-new-queen/truncheon-saturday| title=Canada's New Queen > Truncheon Saturday| publisher=CBC| access-date=8 February 2009}}</ref> In a 1970 speech to the [[Empire Club of Canada]], Governor General [[Roland Michener]] summed up the contemporary arguments against the Crown: From its opponents, he said, came the claims that monarchies are unfashionable, republics—other than those with oppressive regimes—offer more freedom, people are given greater dignity from choosing their head of state, the monarchy is foreign and incompatible with Canada's multicultural society, and that there should be change for the sake of change alone.<ref name=ECF>{{Cite web| last=Michener| first=Roland| author-link=Roland Michener| title=The Empire Club of Canada Speeches 1970–1971| url=http://speeches.empireclub.org/details.asp?SpeechID=562&FT=yes| access-date=10 February 2009| orig-year=19 November 1970| year=1971| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090805165910/http://speeches.empireclub.org/details.asp?SpeechID=562&FT=yes| archive-date=5 August 2009}}</ref> This fits into the argument that the monarchy is not representative of the people of its countries. This has been argued to be the case with Canada having a head of state that is of a foreign nationality and living in another country.<ref>{{cite news |last= Scherer |first= Steve |date= 14 September 2022 |title= More Canadians see monarchy as 'outdated' but political risks block change |url= https://www.yahoo.com/lifestyle/more-canadians-see-monarchy-outdated-050527049.html?guccounter=1 |work= Yahoo! |publisher= Reuters |access-date= 14 September 2022}}</ref>

It was later thought the [[Quiet Revolution]] and the period beyond should have inspired more republicanism amongst Canadians, but it did not.{{#tag:ref|Even prominent calls for a republic, such as those issued by the ''Toronto Star'' editorial board in the [[Canadian Centennial|centennial year of Confederation]], did not inspire action amongst the wider populace. As put by Reg Whitaker: "In the 1960s, in the first fine, careless rapture of bilingualism and biculturalism, an end to the monarchy might have become a shared program between Quebec nationalists and Canadian dualists. It never happened."<ref name=Whitaker14>{{Cite journal |last=Whitaker |first=Reg |date=May 1999 |title=The Monarchy: Gone With the Wind? |url=http://www.irpp.org/po/archive/may99/whitaker.pdf| editor-last=Watson| editor-first=William| journal=Policy Options: Bye-Bye for Good? |page=14| location=Montreal| publisher=Institute for Research on Public Policy| access-date=10 February 2009| archive-date=11 June 2011| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611230730/http://www.irpp.org/po/archive/may99/whitaker.pdf| url-status=dead}}</ref>|group=n|name=Whit}} Reg Whitaker blamed this on a combination of Quebec nationalists having no interest in the monarchy (as full sovereignty and their own form of government was their ultimate goal) with the remainder of the population simultaneously struggling with "bilingualism, dualism, special status, [[distinct society]], asymmetrical federalism, sovereignty-association, partnership, and so on." The rise in multi-ethnic [[immigration to Canada]] in the 1970s did not inspire any significant desire to alter or remove the role of the Crown in Canada, the ethno-cultural groups not wanting to push constitutional change over a matter they had little concern for.<ref name=Whitaker14 />

Instead, until the appointment of [[Stephen Harper]] as prime minister, successive governments made subtle efforts to diminish the stature of the Canadian monarchy<ref name=Coyne>{{cite journal| last=Coyne| first=Andrew| author-link=Andrew Coyne| title=Defending the royals| journal=Maclean's| publisher=Roger's Communications| location=Toronto| date=13 November 2009| url=http://www.macleans.ca/2009/11/13/defending-the-royals/| issn=0024-9262| access-date=18 February 2010}}</ref>—as David Smith said: "the historic Crown with its anthem, emblems, and symbolism made accessible a past the government of the day rejected"<ref>{{Cite book| last=Smith| first=David E.| title=The Invisible Crown| publisher=University of Toronto Press| year=1995| location=Toronto| pages=47| isbn=0-8020-7793-5}}</ref>—though never, since the reaction to some of Prime Minister [[Pierre Trudeau]]'s proposals for alterations to the monarchy and its role in Canada, publicly revealing their stances on the Crown.<ref>{{Cite journal| last=Toporoski| first=Richard| title=The Invisible Crown| journal=Monarchy Canada| publisher=Monarchist League of Canada| location=Toronto| year=1998| url=http://www.monarchist.ca/mc/invisib2.htm| access-date =18 February 2010|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080224145943/http://www.monarchist.ca/mc/invisib2.htm |archive-date = 24 February 2008}}</ref> Following [[Death and state funeral of Queen Elizabeth II|Elizabeth II]]'s death in September 2022, Canadian Prime Minister [[Justin Trudeau]] publicly expressed support for the monarchy's continued status in Canada.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-62957626|title=Prime Minister Justin Trudeau says monarchy offers Canada 'steadiness'|publisher=BBC News|date=September 19, 2022|accessdate=September 19, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.barrons.com/news/canada-s-trudeau-says-monarchy-s-role-not-open-for-debate-01663545006?tesla=y|title=Canada's Trudeau Says Monarchy's Role Not Open For Debate|author=AFP News|publisher=Barron's|date=September 18, 2022|accessdate=September 19, 2022}}</ref>

== Challenges with transitioning to a republic ==
{{copyedit|section|reason=Clunky, poor writing|date=May 2026}}
Due to the unique [[Politics of Canada|political nature]] and [[Structure of the Canadian federal government|structure]] of the Canadian state, there are significant cultural, legal, and constitutional challenges that must be addressed in order for Canada to become a republic. It has been described by political and constitutional law experts as "very difficult" and "virtually impossible" for Canada to remove the Monarch as head of state.<ref name="ctvnews.ca">{{Cite web |date=2022-09-12 |title=Why it would be 'virtually impossible' for Canada to drop the monarchy |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/article/why-it-would-be-virtually-impossible-for-canada-to-drop-the-monarchy/ |access-date=2025-01-09 |website=CTVNews |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-05-11 |title=What Would It Take for Canada to Leave the Monarchy? {{!}} The Walrus |url=https://thewalrus.ca/ask-an-expert-what-would-it-take-to-leave-the-monarchy/ |access-date=2025-01-09 |language=en-US}}</ref>

According to [[Constitution Act, 1982#Part V: Procedure for Amending Constitution of Canada|Part V, section 41, sub-section A]] of the Canadian Constitution Act 1982, any changes to the Monarch's position, including removal, require a constitutional amendment by [[unanimous consent]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-10-26 |title=Canada: Quebec separatist party calls for split with British monarchy |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-63393955 |access-date=2025-01-09 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> This would require the [[House of Commons of Canada|House of Commons]], the [[Senate of Canada|Senate]], and [[Legislative assemblies of Canadian provinces and territories|all 10 of the provincial legislatures]] to vote overwhelmingly for an amendment to remove or amend the role of the Canadian Monarch.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Branch |first=Legislative Services |date=2024-04-09 |title=Consolidated federal laws of Canada, THE CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867 to 1982 |url=https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/const/page-13.html |access-date=2025-01-09 |website=laws-lois.justice.gc.ca}}</ref> Experts argue that this would require a vast amount of [[political capital]] to pass.{{According to whom|date=September 2026}} Despite a somewhat large republican sentiment in the country,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Growing number of Canadians want to reconsider monarchy ties: poll - National {{!}} Globalnews.ca |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/9957136/canada-monarchy-ties-poll/ |access-date=2025-01-09 |website=Global News |language=en-US}}</ref> this capital does not presently exist and the issue is not viewed as a pressing concern; the leaders of the two largest parties, the [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal Party]] and the [[Conservative Party of Canada|Conservatives]], were, as of 2024, publicly supportive of keeping the monarchy.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-04 |title=Let's Keep King Charles to Protect Canadian Democracy - Policy Magazine |url=https://www.policymagazine.ca/lets-keep-king-charles-to-protect-canadian-democracy/ |access-date=2025-01-09 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-09-19 |title=Prime Minister Justin Trudeau says monarchy offers Canada 'steadiness' |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-62957626 |access-date=2025-01-09 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> For instance, a [[Bloc Québécois]]-led republican motion in the House of Commons in 2024 to remove the mention of the King in the parliamentary Oath was voted down and defeated.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tasker |first=John Paul |date=10 Apr 2024 |title=MPs kill bill that would have made oath to King Charles optional |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/mps-kill-bill-change-oath-king-charles-1.7169874 |access-date=9 Jan 2025 |work=CBC News}}</ref> Both constitutional and political challenges would need to be overcome by a republican movement in order for Canada to remove the monarchy, and political and legal experts have stated they "don't see this happening anytime soon."<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |date=2022-01-01 |title=Canada's monarchy ties raise constitutional issues |url=https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/oxan-db272866/full/html |journal=Emerald Expert Briefings |volume=oxan-db |issue=oxan-db |doi=10.1108/OXAN-DB272866 |issn=2633-304X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="ctvnews.ca"/>

Another challenge that also often arises in discussion over the transition to a republic is the treaties and relations with the [[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]] and other [[Indigenous peoples in Canada|Indigenous peoples of Canada]]. Many treaties that have been signed with the indigenous people of Canada were done so between [[the Crown]] and Indigenous nations, not between the Canadian government and Indigenous peoples.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Library |first= |title=Research Guides: Indigenous Treaties: Historic & Numbered Treaties |url=https://guides.library.ubc.ca/indigtreaties/historical |access-date=2025-01-09 |website=guides.library.ubc.ca |language=en}}</ref> This has been reflected in subsequent [[Supreme Court of Canada|Supreme Court]] Rulings such as [[Haida Nation v British Columbia (Minister of Forests)|''Haida Nation v. B.C. (Minister of Forests)'', 2004]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests) - SCC Cases |url=https://decisions.scc-csc.ca/scc-csc/scc-csc/en/item/2189/index.do |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241120222820/https://decisions.scc-csc.ca/scc-csc/scc-csc/en/item/2189/index.do |archive-date=20 November 2024 |access-date=2025-01-09 |website=decisions.scc-csc.ca |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hartley |first=Jackie |date=2005 |title=Case Note: 'Upholding the Honour of the Crown' - Haida Nation v British Columbia (Minister of Forests) |url=https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/journals/IndigLawB/2005/15.html |journal=Indigenous Law Bulletin}}</ref> which reinforced that any dealings by the Canadian government with Indigenous peoples pursuant to the treaties is done so in the name of the Crown. Most experts think consultation with Indigenous peoples on removing the Monarchy should take place prior to any plans for a transition to a republic.<ref name=":0" />

Other challenges that are often raised in discussion of transitioning to a republic include the financial cost associated with removing the monarchy, including changing many [[National symbols of Canada#Official and de facto symbols|Official Canadian National Symbols]], which are widespread across public buildings, institutions, and documents such as passports, changing the appearance of the [[Canadian dollar]], changing the names, insignia, uniforms and rank insignia of the [[Canadian Armed Forces]] and [[Law enforcement in Canada|Police Forces]], as well as the cost of establishing a new republican form of government, amongst others.<ref name="constitutionalstudies.ca">{{Cite web |title=The Monarchy in Canada: God Save the Queen? - Centre for Constitutional Studies |url=https://www.constitutionalstudies.ca/2017/01/the-monarchy-in-canada-god-save-the-queen/?print=print |access-date=2025-01-10 |website=www.constitutionalstudies.ca}}</ref> While some of these costs could arguably be offset in part by the money that is currently spent on the running of the Monarchy in Canada, the Governor General, and Lieutenant Governors (estimated at $58.7 million per year or $1.55 per Canadian Taxpayer,)<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-28 |title=How much does the monarchy cost Canadian taxpayers? |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/article/how-much-does-the-monarchy-cost-canadian-taxpayers/ |access-date=2025-01-10 |website=CTVNews |language=en}}</ref> it is broadly accepted that there would still be a substantial financial cost that would have to be overcome in order to change from Monarchy to Republic.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Canada, the monarchy, and the cost of conceding the Crown |url=https://www.hilltimes.com/story/2022/01/25/canada-the-monarchy-and-the-cost-of-conceding-the-crown/270112/ |access-date=2025-01-10 |website=The Hill Times |language=en-CA}}</ref><ref name="constitutionalstudies.ca"/>

==Democratic principles and governmental role==
Canadian republicans view their country's monarchy as "outdated and irrelevant"<ref name=Freda2003 /> and an undemocratic institution because the incumbent sovereign is neither elected, nor a citizen once on the throne; republicans will phrase this argument as "no Canadian citizen can become head of state."

In contrast to monarchist arguments, those against the Crown assert that it is possible to have an elected head of state be an apolitical individual and there would be no possibility of a clash with the prime minister over differences in political persuasion, though some republicans do desire an empowered chief executive who could hold the Cabinet in check for political reasons. Others feel an appointed Canadian president would be more democratic than the Crown.<ref name=OC /> The range of often contradictory proposals highlights the fact that Canadian republicans are not fully united on what sort of republican form of government they believe the nation should adopt. The Westminster-style parliamentary republican model, which is advocated by other Commonwealth republican movements, has been embraced by Citizens for a Canadian Republic as the preferred model for Canada.
{{Quote box| width=260px| border=1px| align=right| bgcolor=#F5F5DC| quote=''The truth is that the monarchy stands for much that has held Canada back. It embodies the triumph of inheritance over merit, of blood over brains, of mindless ritual over innovation. The monarchy reminds us to defer to authority and remember our place. In Quebec, the Royals are regarded as an insult.''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wente |first=Margaret |author-link=Margaret Wente| date=February 2001 | title=Republican Quotations |website=Monarchy Free Canada| url=http://www.monarchyfreecanada.org/quotations.htm |access-date=24 July 2017 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070310015725/http://www.monarchyfreecanada.org/quotations.htm |archive-date = 10 March 2007}}</ref>| salign=right| source=[[Margaret Wente]], 2001}}

Towards that end, Citizens for a Canadian Republic proposed in March 2004 that the federal [[viceroy]] be made an elected position as a first step towards some form of republic. As the normal channels of appointment would follow after the election, no constitutional reform would be necessary. However, as monarchists point out, the scheme does not take into consideration any provincial input, especially concerning the relationship between the provincial and federal crowns and thus the [[Lieutenant Governor (Canada)|lieutenant governors]]; an issue that would weigh heavily in any constitutional debate on the Crown, regardless of the selection process of the governor general. Further, a 2013 ruling by the Supreme Court of Canada disallowed similar consultative elections for senators, stating that such would be a change to how senators are selected and would thus require a constitutional amendment.<ref>{{cite court| litigants=Governor-in-Council| court=Supreme Court of Canada| date=1 February 2013| url=https://www.macleans.ca/politics/ottawa/for-the-record-the-supreme-court-decision-on-the-senate/| accessdate=8 August 2022}}</ref>

==History of issue==

===Colonial era and Confederation===
{{main|The Reform Movement (Upper Canada)|Rebellions of 1837}}
Reformists began to emerge in the Canadian colonies during the early 19th century and by two decades into that century had begun to cohere into organized groups, such as the Upper Canada Central Political Union. The idea of [[political party]] was viewed by a number of British North Americans as an innovation of the United States, being "anti-British and of a republican tendency." Colonists were warned about "a few individuals, who unfortunately, are led by those, whose hostility to the British constitution is such, that they would sacrifice any and every thing to pull it down, in order that they might build up a Republic on its ruins."<ref>{{cite book| last=Mills| first=David| title=The Idea of Loyalty in Upper Canada, 1784–1850| publisher=McGill-Queen's University Press| year=1988| location=Montreal| pages=77–78| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GuBbZ5PH-hEC&q=%22loyal%20society%22%20canada&pg=PA76| isbn=0-7735-0660-8}}</ref> It was believed that the persons agitating for republican change and their supporters were of American origin and had been taught to admire republican government as the best in the world and ridicule monarchism.<ref>{{Harvnb| Mills| 1988| pp=78–79}}</ref>
[[Image:WLMackenzie1.jpg|thumb|left|[[William Lyon Mackenzie]], founder of the [[Republic of Canada]], and later advocate of Canadian annexation into the [[United States]]]]

The first open uprisings in Canada against the monarchical system came in 1837, with the [[Lower Canada Rebellion]]—led by [[Louis Joseph Papineau]] and his [[Parti canadien|Parti Patriote]]—and the [[Upper Canada Rebellion]]—led by [[William Lyon Mackenzie]]. Though their main motives were for more representative government in their respective colonies, Mackenzie was inspired by the [[Constitution of the United States|American model]] and wished to establish the same in Canada.<ref name=DCBO>{{cite web| url=http://www.biographi.ca/009004-119.01-e.php?&id_nbr=4562&interval=20&&PHPSESSID=ttidfsp0mqgmo2sar6isbmvmu5| last1=Armstrong| first1=Frederick H.| last2=Stagg| first2=Ronald J.| title=Dictionary of Canadian Biography Online > William Lyon Mackenzie| publisher=University of Toronto/Université Laval| year=2000| access-date=8 February 2009}}</ref> Papineau originally expressed loyalty to the Crown in his [[Ninety-Two Resolutions]],<ref>{{cite conference |first=Mary| last=Haslam| title=Ireland and Lower Canada in the early nineteenth century: Love in a time of cholera |conference=The Research Seminar of the Department of French in conjunction with the Centre for the Study of Human Settlement & Historical Change |publisher=National University of Ireland| page=3| date=8 May 2003| version=Paper IV| url=http://www.nuigalway.ie/french/documents/ireland_lower_canada.pdf| access-date=22 August 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040515010049/http://www.nuigalway.ie/french/documents/ireland_lower_canada.pdf| archive-date=15 May 2004}}</ref> but turned when the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|British parliament]] instead adopted [[John Russell, 1st Earl Russell|the Earl Russell]]'s Ten Resolutions, which ignored all 92 of the requests from the Parti Patriote.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/confederation/023001-2002-e.html#developments| last=Library and Archives Canada| author-link=Library and Archives Canada| title=Canadian Confederation > Lower Canada > The Patriot Insurrection (1837–1838)| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=9 February 2009 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080612160458/http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/confederation/023001-2002-e.html#developments |archive-date=12 June 2008}}</ref> Most colonists, however, did not espouse a break with the Crown and the rebellions ultimately failed.<ref name=Philips>{{cite journal|last=Philips |first=Stephen |title=The Emergence of a Canadian Monarchy: 1867–1953 |journal=Canadian Monarchist News |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=1–2 |publisher=Monarchist League of Canada |location=Toronto |date=Summer 2003 |url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2003/CMN_summer_2003_Update-11.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708033423/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2003/CMN_summer_2003_Update-11.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=8 July 2009 |access-date=8 February 2009 }}</ref> Mackenzie fled [[Toronto]] with 200 supporters and established, with the help of [[United States|American]] sympathizers, the short-lived and never recognized [[Republic of Canada]] on [[Navy Island]], while Papineau and other insurgents fled to the United States and proclaimed the [[Republic of Lower Canada]].

After living in the US in order to avoid arrest in Canada, Mackenzie eventually became dissatisfied with the American republican system and gave up plans for revolution in the [[British North America]]n provinces, though he theorized, near the end of his life, on Canadian annexation into the United States, should enough people in the former country become disillusioned with [[responsible government]].<ref name=DCBO /> Similarly, by 1849, Papineau was advocating the absorption of the [[Province of Canada]] (formed in 1840) into the American republic to the south.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.pc.gc.ca/lhn-nhs/qc/papineau/natcul/natcul1a_e.asp| last=Parks Canada| title=Manoir-Papineau National Historic site of Canada > Natural Wonders & Cultural Treasures > A Bit of History > A Chronology of the Life of Louis-Joseph Papineau| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=9 February 2009| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050415225835/http://pc.gc.ca/lhn-nhs/qc/papineau/natcul/natcul1a_E.asp| archive-date=15 April 2005}}</ref> He echoed a significant minority of conservatives in Upper Canada who critiqued Canada's imitation of the [[Westminster system|British parliamentary]] [[constitutional monarchy]] as both too democratic and too tyrannical, theorizing that it simultaneously destroyed the independence of the appointed governor and legislative council and further concentrated power in the Cabinet. Instead, these "republican conservatives" preferred the American federal-state system and the US constitution, seeing the American model of [[checks and balances]] as offering Canada a more fair and conservative form of democracy. They debated constitutional changes that included an elected governor, an elected legislative council, and a possible union with the US, within this republican framework.<ref>{{Cite journal| last=McNairn| first=Jeffrey L.| title=Publius of the North: Tory Republicanism and the American Constitution in Upper Canada, 1848–54| journal=Canadian Historical Review| volume=4| issue=77| pages=504–537| year=1996| issn=0008-3755| doi=10.3138/CHR-077-04-02| s2cid=143826895}}</ref>
[[Image:Louis Riel.jpg|thumb|right|[[Louis Riel]], President of the provisional government of [[Red River of the North|Red River]]]]

Some decades later, in 1869, a [[Red River Rebellion|rebellion in the Red River]] area of [[Rupert's Land]] erupted under the leadership of [[Louis Riel]], who established in the Red River settlement a [[provisional government]] under [[John Bruce (Canada)|John Bruce]] as president, with the intent of negotiating a provincial relationship with the federal government of Canada. As negotiations proceeded, Riel was eventually elected as president by the provisional government's council.  His delegation to [[Ottawa]] was eventually successful in having the [[Monarchy of Canada|federal Crown]]-[[Queen-in-Council|in-Council]] in 1870 found the province of Manitoba with the same parliamentary [[constitutional monarchy]] as existed [[Monarchy in the Canadian provinces|in the other provinces]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.biographi.ca/009004-119.01-e.php?BioId=39918&query=| last=Thomas| first=Lewis H.| title=Dictionary of Canadian Biography Online > Louis Riel| publisher=University of Toronto/Université Laval| year=2000| access-date=9 February 2009}}</ref>

===Post-Quebec sovereignty movement===
The [[Parti Québécois]] rose to power in Quebec on the support of [[Quebec nationalism|nationalists]], with views towards the monarchy that ranged from hostility to indifference. In February 1968, during a [[Constitutional convention (political meeting)|constitutional conference]] in Ottawa, delegates from the [[Union Nationale (Quebec)|Union Nationale]]-governed Quebec indicated that a provincial president might suit the province better than the [[Lieutenant Governor of Quebec|appointed viceroy]]. Two years later, Parti Québécois (PQ) members of the [[National Assembly of Quebec|National Assembly]] refused to recite the constitutionally mandated [[Oath of Allegiance (Canada)|Oath of Allegiance]] to the sovereign before taking their seats in the legislature.<ref name="CBCFLQ"/> Sovereignists protested against the Queen's role in officially opening the [[1976 Summer Olympics|1976 Montreal Olympics]], with [[René Lévesque]] asking Elizabeth to refuse the advice from Prime Minister [[Pierre Trudeau]] and not open the games.<ref name=CBCFLQ /> Republican options were discussed following the election of the sovereigntist Parti Québécois to government in Quebec, but only specifically in relation to the province.<ref name=CBCFLQ>{{cite news| url=https://www.cbc.ca/archives/entry/rene-the-queen-and-the-flq| title=René, The Queen and the FLQ| publisher=CBC| access-date=10 February 2009}}</ref>

Continuing talks of constitutional reform led to the role of the monarchy in Canada coming under scrutiny in the lead up to the [[patriation]] of the [[Constitution of Canada|Canadian constitution]] in 1982.<ref>{{Cite journal| last=Heinricks| first=Geoff |year=2001| title=Trudeau and the Monarchy| journal=Canadian Monarchist News| publisher=Monarchist League of Canada, reprinted courtesy National Post| publication-date=July 2001| location=Toronto| issue=Winter/Spring 2001–2001| url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2001/opinion.htm |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080622173849/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2001/opinion.htm |archive-date = 22 June 2008 |access-date=24 July 2017}}</ref><ref name=Smith11>{{Harvard citation|Smith|1999| p=11}}</ref> However, proposals for change were thwarted by the provinces, including Quebec.<ref name=Phillips19 /><ref name=Smith11 /><ref>{{Cite journal | last=Valpy| first=Michael| title=Don't Mess With Success – and Good Luck Trying| url=http://www.irpp.org/po/archive/may99/valpy.pdf| editor-last=Watson| editor-first=William| periodical=Policy Options: Bye-Bye for Good?| date=May 1999| pages=26| location=Montreal| publisher=Institute for Research on Public Policy| access-date=17 February 2009| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120217112947/http://www.irpp.org/po/archive/may99/valpy.pdf| archive-date=17 February 2012}}</ref>

The notion of a republic was raised publicly in the early 1990s, when [[Peter C. Newman]] wrote in ''Maclean's'' that the monarchy should be abolished in favour of a head of state "who would reflect our own, instead of imported, values." Then, in 1997, [[Deputy Prime Minister of Canada|Deputy Prime Minister]] [[John Manley (politician)|John Manley]] echoed Newman when he expressed at the end of a television interview his opinion that Canada should abolish its monarchy, citing Australia's contemporary discussions around the [[Monarchy of Australia|Australian Crown]].<ref name=CMNManley>{{cite journal|last=Aimers |first=John |author-link=John Aimers |title=John Manley: Republican |journal=Canadian Monarchist News |issue=Autumn 1998 |publisher=Monarchist League of Canada |location=Toronto |year=1998 |url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/1998/manley.htm |access-date=13 February 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708001344/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/1998/manley.htm |archive-date=8 July 2009 }}</ref> Then, in December of the following year, the Prime Minister's press secretary, [[Peter Donolo]], who also complained that the monarch made Canada appear as a "colonial outpost",<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Victoria Day Public Forum: Canada After the Queen |publisher=Citizens for a Canadian Republic |date=18 May 2009 |url=http://www.canadian-republic.ca/pdf_files/CCR_Poster_5-18-09.pdf |access-date=13 January 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220304054400/http://www.canadian-republic.ca/pdf_files/CCR_Poster_5-18-09.pdf |archive-date=4 March 2022 |url-status=dead}}</ref> unaccountably announced through a media story that the [[Office of the Prime Minister (Canada)|Prime Minister's Office]] was considering the abolition of the monarchy as a millennium project, though no definitive plans had been made.<ref name=CBC1>{{cite news|title=Liberals considering break from monarchy |publisher=CBC |date=18 December 1998 |url=https://www.cbc.ca/archives/entry/rene-the-queen-and-the-flq |access-date=11 February 2009}}</ref> Donolo later supported Manley when,<small>{{#tag:ref|Donolo wrote in ''[[Maclean's]]'' that "it's the institution of the monarchy that is incompatible with the values of a modern, democratic, pluralistic state."<ref name=Journals>{{cite journal| last=Various| title=Views of the Royal Homecoming| journal=Canadian Monarchist News| issue=Spring 2002| publisher=Monarchist League of Canada| location=Toronto| year=2002| url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2002/03spring004.html| access-date=14 February 2009| archive-date=8 July 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708034420/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2002/03spring004.html| url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Throngs>{{cite journal| title=Throngs Hail Canada's Golden Queen| journal=Canadian Monarchist News| issue=Autumn 2002| publisher=Monarchist League of Canada| location=Toronto| year=2002| url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2002/03spring001.html| access-date=11 February 2009| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708003353/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2002/03spring001.html| archive-date=8 July 2009}}</ref>|group=n|name=Donolo}}</small> on [[Victoria Day]] 2001, Manley said on CBC Radio that he believed that hereditary succession was outdated, and that the country's head of state should be elected.<ref name="cbc.ca">{{cite news| title=Canada no longer needs Queen: Manley| publisher=CBC| date=18 May 2001| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/canada-no-longer-needs-queen-manley-1.283675| access-date=18 February 2009}}</ref> Then, just prior to the Queen's pan-country tour to celebrate [[Golden Jubilee of Elizabeth II|her Golden Jubilee]] the following year, Manley (at that point the designated minister in attendance for the sovereign's arrival in Ottawa) again stated his preference for a "wholly Canadian" institution to replace the present monarchy after the reign of Queen Elizabeth II;<ref name="Hunter 2002">{{Cite news| last=Hunter| first=Stuart| title=British Columbians outraged at Manley| newspaper=The Province| date=7 October 2002}}</ref> he was rebuked by other Cabinet members, a former prime minister, and the Leader of the Opposition,<ref name=Throngs /> as well as a number of prominent journalists.<small>{{#tag:ref|Negative commentary came from [[John Fraser (journalist)|John Fraser]] and Christie Blachford in the ''[[National Post]]'', Rosie DiManno in the ''[[Toronto Star]]'', Hartley Steward in ''The Sunday Sun'', [[Michael Valpy]] in ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'',<ref name="Journals"/><ref name="Throngs"/> [[Rex Murphy]] on the [[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation|CBC]],<ref name="Murphy">{{Cite news |last=Murphy |first=Rex |url=http://www.cbc.ca/national/rex/rex20021007.html |title=Manley and the monarchy |date=7 October 2002 |work=The National |access-date=11 February 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030220133221/http://www.cbc.ca/national/rex/rex20021007.html |archive-date=20 February 2003 |publisher=CBC News}}</ref> and [[Andrew Coyne]] in the [[National Post]].<ref name=NP>{{Cite news| last=Coyne| first=Andrew| author-link=Andrew Coyne| title=A lightning rod for patriotic love| newspaper=National Post| date=10 April 2002| url=http://andrewcoyne.com/columns/NationalPost/2002/20020410.html| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060523040653/http://andrewcoyne.com/columns/NationalPost/2002/20020410.html| archive-date=23 May 2006}}</ref>|group=n|name=Journs}}</small>

In 2002, the group [[Citizens for a Canadian Republic]] was established to promote the abolition of the Canadian monarchy in favour of a republic, at approximately the same time ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'' newspaper began a campaign against the monarchy,<ref name="Senex 2007 23">{{cite journal| last=Senex| title=The "News" Columns of "Canada's National Newspaper"| journal=Canadian Monarchist News| volume=Summer 2007| issue=26| page=23| publisher=Monarchist League of Canada| location=Toronto| year=2007| url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2007/Summer_2007_CMN.pdf| access-date=26 July 2009|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080625225416/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2007/Summer_2007_CMN.pdf |archive-date = 25 June 2008}}</ref> with three republican journalists on staff{{spaced ndash}}[[Margaret Wente]], [[Jeffrey Simpson]],<ref name="Simpson"/> and [[Lawrence Martin (journalist)|Lawrence Martin]]<ref name="Martin"/>{{spaced ndash}}though the editorial board argued Canada could dispose of its monarchy without becoming a republic. Tom Freda, chairman and co-founder of Citizens for a Canadian Republic, called for simply replacing the monarchy with the governor general, saying that he's not in favour of destroying Canada's identity or cultural institutions: "All we're advocating is that the link to the monarchy, in our Constitution, be severed. Our governor general for the past 60 years has performed all the duties of a head of state, and there's no reason we shouldn't make our governor general our official head of state."<ref>{{cite news| last=Berenyi| first=Valerie| title=Raise a tall, cold one to the Queen| journal=Calgary Herald | date=17 May 2009| url=http://www2.canada.com/calgaryherald/news/story.html?id=33d7836f-ab04-4511-b9e0-458d0f409487&p=3| issn=0024-9262| access-date=3 July 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141031012129/http://www2.canada.com/calgaryherald/news/story.html?id=33d7836f-ab04-4511-b9e0-458d0f409487&p=3| archive-date=31 October 2014}}</ref> Freda also, however, called the governor general and lieutenant governors "redundant".<ref>{{citation| url=https://edmonton.citynews.ca/2020/09/18/should-canada-cut-ties-with-the-british-monarchy/| last=Craddock| first=Derek| title=Should Canada cut ties with the British monarchy?| date=18 September 2020| publisher=CityNews| accessdate=8 August 2022}}</ref>

At approximately the same time, the editors of ''The Globe and Mail'' began calling for the governor general to be made head of state under the guise of "patriating the monarchy", and arguing that Canada could rid itself of its Crown without becoming a republic,<ref name="Senex 2007 23"/> and backing their journalist [[Jeffrey Simpson]]'s preference for the Companions of the [[Order of Canada]] to choose the head of state in a Canadian republic.<ref name=Simpson>{{Cite news| last1=Simpson| first1=Jeffrey| author-link=Jeffrey Simpson| last2=Valpy| first2=Michael| author2-link=Michael Valpy| title=Has the magic gone out of our monarchy?| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| pages=F6| date=13 April 2002| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/servlet/GIS.Servlets.HTMLTemplate?tf=tgam/common/FullStory.html&cf=tgam/common/FullStory.cfg&date=20020413&cache_key=internationalAfricaHeadline&current_row=4&start_row=4&num_rows=1| location=Toronto| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060815130149/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/servlet/GIS.Servlets.HTMLTemplate?tf=tgam%2Fcommon%2FFullStory.html| archive-date=15 August 2006}}</ref>

[[Lawrence Martin (journalist)|Lawrence Martin]] called for Canada to become a republic in order to re-brand the nation and better its standings in the international market, he cited [[Sweden]] – a constitutional monarchy – as an example to be followed.<ref name="Martin">{{Cite news| last=Martin| first=Lawrence| author-link=Lawrence Martin (journalist)| title=Wallflowers, it's time for a new stage of nationhood| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| date=29 July 2007| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/servlet/Page/document/v5/content/subscribe?user_URL=https://www.theglobeandmail.com%2Fservlet%2Fstory%2FRTGAM.20070729.comartin30%2FBNStory%2FFront%2Fhome&ord=2734943&brand=theglobeandmail&force_login=true| location=Toronto}}</ref>

In 2007, Quebec sovereignty again collided with the monarchy, when Quebec separatists threatened to mount demonstrations should the Queen be in attendance at the ceremonies for the [[400th anniversary of Quebec City]]; [[Mario Beaulieu]], then vice-president of the [[Saint-Jean-Baptiste Society]] announced that the Queen's presence would be a catalyst for action, saying: "You can be sure that people will demonstrate in protest... We are celebrating the foundation of [[New France]], not its conquest. The monarchy remains a symbol of imperialism and colonialism. Her presence will not be welcomed", and Gérald Larose, president of the Quebec Sovereignty Council, stated that the monarchy was "the most despicable, appalling, anti-democratic, imperial, colonial symbol against which all social and individuals rights were obtained through the course of history."<ref>{{Cite news| last=Séguin| first=Rhéal| title=A birthday visit by the Queen? Quebeckers are not amused| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| date=13 April 2007| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/servlet/Page/document/v5/content/subscribe?user_URL=https://www.theglobeandmail.com%2Fservlet%2Fstory%2FRTGAM.20070413.wqueen0414%2FBNStory%2FNational%2Fhome&ord=27749045&brand=theglobeandmail| access-date=17 February 2009| location=Toronto}}</ref>

At the [[Liberal Party of Canada]] convention in January 2012, its members debated on a motion to include severing ties with the monarchy as a party platform.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/politics/article/1109852--liberals-to-ponder-severing-canada-s-ties-to-the-monarchy | location=Toronto | work=The Star | first=Susan | last=Delacourt | title=Young Liberals want to cut royal ties | date=3 January 2012}}</ref> The proposed motion was rejected by 67%<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mas |first=Susana |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/liberals-choose-renewal-in-electing-crawley-1.1220395 |title=Liberals choose renewal in electing Crawley |date=15 January 2012}}</ref>

On October 26, 2022, [[Bloc Québécois]] (BQ) Leader [[Yves-François Blanchet]] moved a motion calling for the severing of "ties between the Canadian State and the British monarchy" in the Federal [[House of Commons of Canada|House of Commons]], It was rejected 44 to 266.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vote Detail - 199 - Members of Parliament - House of Commons of Canada |url=https://www.ourcommons.ca/members/en/votes/44/1/199 |access-date=2023-06-28 |website=www.ourcommons.ca}}</ref>

==Activities==
As abolition of the monarchy would require a constitutional amendment made only after the achievement of unanimous consent amongst the [[Parliament of Canada|federal parliament]] and all ten [[Legislative Assemblies of Canadian provinces and territories|provincial legislatures]], republicans face difficulty in achieving their goal.<ref>{{cite journal| last=Ritchie| first=Jonathan |author2=Markwell, Don | title=Australian and Commonwealth Republicanism| journal=The Round Table| volume=95| issue=5| page=733| publisher=Routledge| location=Newtownabbey| date=October 2006| issn=0035-8533| doi=10.1080/00358530601046976| s2cid=154734100 }}</ref> Further, though republicans have pointed to [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]] and [[India]] as models that could be adapted to Canada, no specific form of republic or selection method for a president has been decided on,<ref>{{Cite news| last=Ward| first=John| title=Canadian anti-monarchists watch Aussie debate| newspaper=Toronto Star| date=10 April 2009| url=https://www.thestar.com/article/616826| access-date=15 September 2009}}</ref> and the Canadian populace remains largely indifferent to the issue.<ref>{{Harvnb| Whitaker| 1999| p=12}}</ref>

Up until 2010, most republican action had taken the form of protests on [[Victoria Day]]{{spaced ndash}}the Canadian sovereign's [[Birthday#Official birthdays|official birthday]]{{spaced ndash}}in [[Toronto]], lobbying of the federal and provincial governments to eliminate [[Canadian royal symbols]],<ref>{{cite press release| title=Time to Promote Canada not Queen on Holiday| publisher=Citizens for a Canadian Republic| date=20 May 2004| url=https://www.canadian-republic.ca/media_release_5_20_04| access-date=22 May 2022}}</ref> and legal action against the Crown, specifically in relation to the [[Oath of Citizenship (Canada)|Oath of Citizenship]] and the [[Act of Settlement 1701]].<ref>{{cite press release| title=Canada's Republican Movement Presents Legal Case Against the Monarchy| publisher=Citizens for a Canadian Republic| date=24 September 2002| url=https://www.canadian-republic.ca/media_release_9_24_02| access-date=22 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release| title=Oath to Queen Costs Canada Citizens, Says Republican Movement| publisher=Citizens for a Canadian Republic| date=5 November 2002| url=https://www.canadian-republic.ca/media_release_11_05_02| access-date=22 May 2022}}</ref>

Today, most of [[Citizens for a Canadian Republic]]'s activities are educational, providing commentators to the media and networking with supporters in all political parties.<ref name=CCRabout>{{cite web| url=https://www.canadian-republic.ca/about| title=About| publisher=Citizens for a Canadian Republic| access-date=22 May 2022}}</ref>

In 2013, several former members of Citizens for a Canadian Republic formed Republic Now, led by Ashok Charles, which has a more activist approach in advocating for a republic.<ref>{{cite news |title=Anti-monarchy group raising cash for ad campaign |url=https://torontosun.com/2016/05/21/anti-monarchy-group-raising-cash-for-ad-campaign |access-date=January 3, 2024 |newspaper=Toronto Sun |date=May 21, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Should Queen Elizabeth II Be Canada's Last Monarch? |url=https://thewalrus.ca/should-queen-elizabeth-be-canadas-last-monarch/ |access-date=January 3, 2024 |work=The Walrus |date=June 28, 2017}}</ref>

[[Ted McWhinney]] has argued that Canada can become a republic upon the demise of the current monarch by not proclaiming a successor; according to McWhinney, this would be a way for the constitution to evolve "more subtly and by indirection, through creating new glosses on the Law of the Constitution as written, without formally amending it."<ref>{{Cite news| last=Yaffe| first=Barbara| title=Ditching royals is easy, expert says| newspaper=Vancouver Sun| date=17 February 2005}}</ref> However, Ian Holloway, Dean of Law at the [[University of Western Ontario]], criticized this proposal for its ignorance of provincial input, and opined that its implementation "would be contrary to the plain purpose of those who framed our system of government."<ref>{{Cite journal| last=Holloway| first=Ian| date=Spring 2005 |title=Liberal Stalking Horse for Stealth Ending of Monarchy? | periodical=Canadian Monarchist News |issue=23| page=2| location=Toronto| publisher=Monarchist League of Canada| url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2005/Spring_2005_CMN.pdf| access-date=18 May 2009| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080625225427/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2005/Spring_2005_CMN.pdf| archive-date=25 June 2008}}</ref>

== Opinion polling ==
{{POV section| date=March 2024}}
{{see also|Debate on the monarchy in Canada#Polls}}
Polls conducted on the subject of abolition of the Canadian Crown in 2022 and 2023, following the [[Proclamation of accession of Charles III|accession of Charles III]], stated that 58% of Canadians think there should be a referendum on the future of the monarchy and between 40% and 54% of Canadians favour becoming a republic.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.ipsos.com/en-ca/news-polls/canadians-conflicted-on-future-role-of-monarchy |title= Canadians Conflicted on Future Role of Monarchy as Half (54%) Say Canada Should End Ties to Monarchy |last= |first= |date= 16 September 2022 |website= ipsos.com |publisher= Ipsos |access-date= 15 February 2024}}</ref><ref name="ashcroft">{{Cite web |date=3 May 2023 |title=New poll reveals why Canadians won't abolish the monarchy even though they don't like it |url=https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/canadians-king-charles-monarchy-poll |website=nationalpost.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Polls (LordAshcroftPolls.com) |first=Lord Ashcroft |title=LORD ASHCROFT POLLS : AHEAD OF CORONATION, NEW POLL FINDS CANADA WOULD VOTE TO BECOME A REPUBLIC - BUT MOST SAY OTHER ISSUES MATTER MORE |url=https://www.newswire.ca/news-releases/lord-ashcroft-polls-ahead-of-coronation-new-poll-finds-canada-would-vote-to-become-a-republic-but-most-say-other-issues-matter-more-888366124.html |access-date=2023-10-16 |website=www.newswire.ca |language=en}}</ref> However, pollster [[Michael Ashcroft]] cautioned that, "for change to happen in Canada, the issue would have to find its way to the top of the political agenda. It’s hard to see what could be the catalyst for that to happen."<ref name="ashcroft"/>

In 2025, on the eve of King Charles III and Queen Camilla's visit to Canada, a poll released by [[Pollara|Pollara Strategic Insights]] showed that 45% of Canadians support retaining the monarchy, while 39% favour ending ties to the crown.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.pollara.com/canadians-warming-to-king-charles-and-the-monarchy/ |title= Canadians warming to King Charles and the monarchy |last= |first= |date= 25 May 2025 |website= Pollara.com |publisher= Pollara |access-date= 25 May 2025}}</ref>
